defs.text: The actual, substantial presence of the body of Christ with the bread and wine of the sacrament of the Lord's Supper; impanation; -- opposed to transubstantiation. Note: This view, held by Luther himself, was called consubstantiation by non Lutheran writers in contradistinction to transsubstantiation, the Catholic view.

Consubstantiation.note: Lutheran churches generally don't use this word for their own teaching and speak of a sacramental union.

defs.head: Dispensationalism
defs.text: adherence to or advocacy of a system of interpreting history in terms of a series of God's dispensations

Dispensationalism.note: This is a view held by some Protestants, particularly among conservative evangelicals. Covenant theologians and many other Christians reject it.

defs.text: That which is taught; what is held, put forth as true, and supported by a teacher, a school, or a sect; a principle or position, or the body of principles, in any branch of knowledge; any tenet or dogma; a principle of faith

defs.head: Ecclesiology
defs.text: theological doctrine relating to the church
The criminality and consequent exposure to punishment resulting from willful disobedience of law, or from morally wrong action

defs.source: John A. Hardon, Modern Catholic Dictionary, “Kenosis”, on CatholicCulture.org
defs.head: Kenosis
defs.text: The voluntary renunciation by Christ of his right to divine privilege in his humble acceptance of human status.

Kenosis.note: The word comes from Philippians 2:7, “emptied himself.” Christians agree He remained God and differ on what the emptying involved. Some modern “kenotic” theories hold that He set aside divine attributes, which many theologians reject.

defs.source: Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Monarchianism”, as reproduced on Wikisource
defs.head: Monarchianism
defs.text: a theological term designating the view taken by those Christians who, within the Church, towards the end of the 2nd century and during the 3rd, opposed the doctrine of an independent personal subsistence of the Logos.

Monarchianism.note: It is usually divided into two kinds, dynamic (see Adoptionism) and modalistic (see Modalism). Mainstream churches rejected both.

defs.text: The doctrine or belief that there is but one God.
The act of obeying, or the state of being obedient; compliance with that which is required by authority; subjection to rightful restraint or control.
The act of setting apart to an office in the Christian ministry; the conferring of holy orders.

defs.source: Edward Hanna, “Purgatory”, The Catholic Encyclopedia, vol. 12 (1911), on New Advent
defs.head: Purgatory
defs.text: Purgatory (Lat., "purgare", to make clean, to purify) in accordance with Catholic teaching is a place or condition of temporal punishment for those who, departing this life in God's grace, are, not entirely free from venial faults, or have not fully paid the satisfaction due to their transgressions.

Purgatory.note: This is Catholic teaching. Protestant churches reject it, and Orthodox churches don't teach it in this form.

defs.head: Rapture
defs.text: the final assumption of Christians into heaven during the end-time according to some Christian theologies

Rapture.note: Christians differ on this. Dispensationalists teach a separate event before the return of Christ, while many others read 1 Thessalonians 4:17 as part of His one return.

defs.text: Discharge from that which is due; relinquishment of a claim, right, or obligation; pardon of transgression; release from forfeiture, penalty, debt, etc.
The spiritual, rational, and immortal part in man; that part of man which enables him to think, and which renders him a subject of moral government

Soul.note: Christians differ on whether soul and spirit are two parts of a person or two words for one.

defs.source: Murray's New English Dictionary (1919), “Subordinationism”, on the World English Historical Dictionary
defs.head: Subordinationism
defs.text: The doctrine that the second and third persons of the Trinity are inferior, in order or in essence, to the first person.

Subordinationism.note: The Nicene Creed rejects inferiority in essence. Whether the Son's obedience implies any eternal ordering is still debated.

defs.text: A manifestation of God to man by actual appearance, usually as an incarnation.
